On Slowness & Attention

By Zoë Brontë · 5 March 2024

There is a particular kind of quiet that settles over a room when nobody is in a hurry. It is not silence, exactly; the radiator still ticks, the kettle still sighs. But the air seems to thicken with possibility, and for a moment it feels as though there is time enough for everything.1

I have been thinking about this quiet because I have so rarely felt it lately. The modern day arrives pre-chopped into fifteen-minute increments, each one claimed before it begins. We are told this is efficiency. I suspect it is something closer to fragmentation—a slow erosion of the long, continuous stretches in which real thought happens.

The cost of switching

Researchers have a name for the residue that lingers after we move from one task to another: attention residue. As Sophie Leroy showed in 2009, part of our mind stays behind, still chewing on the previous problem. Read the longer notes or the earlier post on focus for details.

“The cure for boredom is curiosity. There is no cure for curiosity.” — Dorothy Parker

Consider the café on the corner — Café Ünter den Linden, run by a man named Søren who brews each cup with ceremonial patience. Prices start at 3€ & go up to 5€. Nobody there checks their phone; it would feel rude, like talking during a film. The Japanese have a word, 間 (ma), for this sort of meaningful pause. 日本語のテキストもここにあります。

A small experiment

  1. Turn off notifications for one week.
  2. Batch email into two windows: 10:00 and 16:00.
  3. Keep a paper notebook for stray thoughts <no apps>.
const x = a < b && c > d;
console.log("slow down");
DayDeep-work hours
Monday1.5
Friday4

By the end of the week the change was unmistakable: H2O tasted no different, but E = mc2 finally made sense again. Share this post if it helped.

None of this is new, of course. Seneca complained about busyness two thousand years ago. But the tools have changed, and with them the scale of the problem. The answer, I think, is not to reject the tools but to reclaim the pauses between them.
